note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Explain what generative AI is and is not

evidence.title: Short explainer of generative AI and its limits
evidence.example: You write a 300-word explainer, in your own words, on how a generative AI chatbot produces text by predicting likely words from patterns in its training data. Drawing on Bender and colleagues' (2021) "stochastic parrots" critique, you explain why fluent output is not the same as understanding or a checked fact (for example, why a chatbot can invent a plausible reference for a biology topic). This shows you can say what generative AI is and is not.
evidence.artefact: A 300-word explainer in your own words with one worked example of a fabricated or wrong AI answer.
grounding: model: Stochastic parrots critique of large language models (Bender et al. 2021)

evidence.title: Explaining AI to visitors as a student ambassador
evidence.example: As a student ambassador at an open day, you are asked by a parent whether students just use AI to write essays. You give a short, accurate answer on what generative AI is, what it cannot be relied on for, and that universities set rules on its use (for example, explaining to a prospective computing student that AI predicts text rather than looking facts up).
evidence.artefact: Your prepared talking points and a short note from the ambassador coordinator who observed the conversation.
grounding: practice: student ambassador role at an open day

genericOutcomes.title: Concept map of a digital tool's capabilities and limits
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain what a generative AI tool can and cannot reliably do, distinguishing genuine capability from assumption.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a digital tool that is central to a field of work, you set out, in a short written piece, what the tool can reliably do, what it cannot do, and the boundary between the two. You draw on an established account of how the technology actually works, rather than on marketing claims or assumption, to support each point you make. This demonstrates using a core digital tool only after genuinely understanding its capabilities and limits.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A one-page concept map setting out the tool's genuine capabilities, its limits and the reasoning behind each.
grounding: model: Stochastic parrots critique of large language models (Bender et al. 2021)

genericOutcomes.title: Briefing explaining a digital tool's capabilities to colleagues
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can brief others on what a digital tool can be trusted to do and what checks they should still carry out before relying on it.
genericOutcomes.example: A digital tool that a field depends on is being introduced to people who will use it day to day, and you are asked to brief them before they start. You explain, in plain terms, what the tool can be trusted to do, what it cannot, and the checks they should still carry out themselves before relying on it. This demonstrates using the digital tools a field relies on competently and helping others do the same.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The briefing notes you prepared, with a short summary of the questions colleagues asked afterwards.
grounding: professional: Explains a digital tool's genuine capabilities and limits to colleagues before they rely on it.

capabilities.statement: Check the assessment guidance before using AI

evidence.title: Mapping a module's AI rule to its learning outcomes
evidence.example: Before using any AI tool, you read your module's AI statement and its learning outcomes side by side. Using Biggs' (1996) constructive alignment, you explain in a few sentences why the rule fits what the task is assessing (for example, why a first-year economics essay bans AI for drafting because the outcome is your own argument). This shows you check the guidance first and understand why the rule exists.
evidence.artefact: A one-page table linking each part of the AI statement to a learning outcome, with your short explanation.

evidence.title: Clarifying AI guidance with a tutor before an assignment
evidence.example: Before starting a first-year business assignment, you find the AI statement for that task and note what is allowed and what is not. Where it is unclear, you email your tutor a specific question and keep the reply (for example, whether you may use AI to check your grammar in a group report). This shows you check the assessment guidance before using AI.
evidence.artefact: The task's AI statement with your annotations, your question to the tutor and the tutor's reply.

genericOutcomes.title: Explanation of why a digital use rule fits its purpose
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain why a rule governing permitted digital tools for a task connects to what that task is meant to demonstrate.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a rule governing which digital tools may be used for a piece of work, you set out, in a short written account, the reasoning that connects the rule to what the work is meant to demonstrate. You draw on an established model of aligning method with intended outcome to show the rule is not arbitrary or accidental. This demonstrates understanding the digital tools and technologies a field relies on, and why their use is sometimes restricted.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account linking a digital use rule to its underlying purpose, using a named model.

genericOutcomes.title: Checklist confirming permitted tools before starting a task
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can draw up and resolve, in writing, a checklist of permitted and restricted digital tools before starting a task.
genericOutcomes.example: Before beginning a piece of work, you draw up a short checklist of which digital tools and technologies are permitted, which are restricted, and where the boundary is unclear. You resolve any unclear point in writing before you start, rather than assuming, and you keep the checklist together with your finished work. This demonstrates using the digital tools and technologies a field relies on, within its stated rules.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Your checklist of permitted and restricted tools, with any written clarification you obtained before starting.
grounding: professional: Confirms which digital tools are permitted for a task before relying on any of them.

capabilities.statement: Recognise what AI cannot be trusted for, and think first

evidence.title: Think-first comparison of your answer and an AI answer
evidence.example: You answer a short study question yourself first, then, where permitted, compare your answer with a chatbot's. Using Flavell's (1979) idea of metacognitive monitoring, you note where you were confident, where the AI was wrong or vague, and what it cannot be trusted for (for example, current legal thresholds in a first-year law topic). This shows you recognise the limits of AI and of your own knowledge, and think before relying on it.
evidence.artefact: A short reflective log entry showing your own answer, the AI answer, the checks you made and what you concluded.

evidence.title: Deciding not to rely on AI in a gym job
evidence.example: Working part time at a gym, a member asks you for a diet plan for a health condition. You recognise that a chatbot cannot be trusted for individual health advice, think through what you know and do not know, and refer the member to a qualified colleague (for example, someone managing diabetes asking about pre-training meals). This shows you know when AI should not be relied on.
evidence.artefact: A brief workplace log entry recording the request, why you did not use AI and who you referred the member to.
grounding: practice: part-time job in a gym

genericOutcomes.title: Monitoring log of confidence before trusting a digital tool
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify, before relying on a digital tool's answer, where their own understanding falls short and where the tool's output cannot be trusted.
genericOutcomes.example: Before relying on a digital tool to answer a question in a field you are learning, you note your own level of confidence and understanding first. You then test the tool's answer against that starting point, using an established account of monitoring your own thinking, and record where the tool's output could not be trusted. This demonstrates judging where the digital tools a field relies on fall short, before using them.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short monitoring log recording your starting confidence, the tool's answer and where it could not be trusted.

genericOutcomes.title: Record of a request a digital tool should not handle
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can recognise a type of request that a standard digital tool should not be trusted to answer and set out what to do instead.
genericOutcomes.example: You identify a type of request that the standard digital tools in your field should not be used to answer, because it needs judgement a tool cannot supply. You think the request through yourself, note exactly why the tool is unsuitable for it, and set out what you did instead of relying on the tool. This demonstrates recognising the limits of the digital tools and technologies a field relies on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written record of the request, the reasoning for not using the tool, and the alternative you used.
grounding: professional: Identifies requests that fall outside what a standard digital tool should be trusted to answer.

capabilities.statement: Apply a critical-use workflow, AI as a critical friend

evidence.title: Critical friend prompt log on your own draft
evidence.example: Where your task permits it, you ask an AI tool to question a draft you have already written, not to write it. Using Costa and Kallick's (1993) idea of a critical friend who asks provoking questions and offers critique, you record each prompt, what the AI suggested and whether you accepted or rejected it, with reasons (for example, a geography essay where you rejected an invented statistic). This shows you use AI critically while the thinking stays yours.
evidence.artefact: A prompt-and-decision log beside your draft, with your disclosure statement and reasons for each accepted or rejected suggestion.

evidence.title: Using permitted AI to review copy on a placement
evidence.example: On a marketing placement where your manager allows a company-approved AI tool, you write campaign copy yourself, then use the tool to test it for tone and clarity. You verify its claims, keep your own judgement on what the client needs and tell your manager how you used it (for example, rejecting a suggested health claim the product cannot support).
evidence.artefact: A dated decision log of AI suggestions you kept or rejected, with your manager's note confirming the tool was approved.
grounding: professional: Uses AI to draft, question and check work while keeping professional judgement and verifying output.

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoned judgement after an AI tool questions a draft
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate challenges raised by an AI tool against the actual evidence to reach a reasoned judgement that remains their own.
genericOutcomes.example: You give an AI tool a piece of reasoning you have already drafted and ask it to challenge the weakest points, rather than to produce new content. You weigh each challenge against the evidence you actually have, decide which points genuinely need revising, and set out the reasoning behind each decision you reach. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a judgement that is still your own.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account of the AI's challenges, your evaluation of each, and your final reasoned position.

genericOutcomes.title: Verified judgement reached with AI acting as challenger
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can use an AI tool to question a piece of work, test each challenge against the evidence, and justify which points to revise.
genericOutcomes.example: Before finishing a piece of work, you use an AI tool to question your reasoning and flag claims that look weak or unsupported. You test each flagged point against the actual evidence available, decide what to change and what to keep, and record a brief justification for each call you make. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically, using AI to probe rather than replace your own judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of the AI's challenges, your evaluation of each, and the justification for your final decisions.
grounding: professional: Uses AI to draft, question and check work while keeping professional judgement and verifying output.

capabilities.statement: Fact-check AI output and disclose its use

evidence.title: Lateral reading verification table for AI output
evidence.example: Where AI use is permitted, you take five factual claims from an AI answer and check each one by lateral reading: leaving the output to see what reliable sources say, as described by Wineburg and McGrew (2019). You record which claims held, which were wrong and the source you will cite instead (for example, drug dosage claims in a pharmacy task). You then write a clear disclosure of how you used AI.
evidence.artefact: A verification table of claims, checks and outcomes, with the disclosure statement you attached to your work.

evidence.title: Fact-checked, disclosed AI use in a coding assignment
evidence.example: In a computing assignment that allows AI to explain error messages, you test every AI suggestion against the official documentation before using it. You note what was wrong or outdated and write a disclosure statement in the format your department requires (for example, an AI explanation that relied on a deprecated library function). This shows you fact-check AI output and disclose its use honestly.
evidence.artefact: Your submitted disclosure statement and a testing log showing each AI suggestion, how you checked it and the result.
grounding: practice: permitted AI use in a programming assignment

genericOutcomes.title: Verification record for a digital tool's factual output
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse why a digital tool's factual claims require verification against an independent source before being accepted.
genericOutcomes.example: A digital tool you are learning to use produces a factual claim as part of its output, and instead of accepting it, you check it against an independent, reliable source. Using an established method for verifying information away from where it was first encountered, you record what you found and whether the claim held up. This demonstrates using a digital tool a field relies on while still checking what it produces.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short verification record showing the claim checked, the independent source used and the outcome.

genericOutcomes.title: Disclosed, verified use of a digital tool's output
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can check a digital tool's factual output against an independent source and disclose clearly how and where the tool was used.
genericOutcomes.example: After a digital tool produces output you intend to use, you check its factual claims against an independent source before relying on any of them. You keep a short record of what you checked and what you found, and you disclose clearly, in the finished work, exactly how and where the tool was used. This demonstrates using the digital tools a field relies on responsibly and transparently.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A verification record of the claims checked, plus the disclosure statement describing how the tool was used.
grounding: professional: Checks a digital tool's factual output against an independent source and discloses how the tool was used.

capabilities.statement: Decide, with reasons, when and when not to use AI

evidence.title: Forethought decision record on AI use for one task
evidence.example: Before starting a substantial assignment, you write a decision record on whether and how to use AI. Using the forethought phase of Zimmerman's (2002) self-regulated learning cycle, you set your goals, weigh what AI would help and what it would take away from your learning, and check the rules (for example, a psychology report where you use AI only to test your search terms). You revisit the decision afterwards.
evidence.artefact: A one-page decision record with your reasons, the rule you checked and a short review written after submission.

evidence.title: Society decision on AI for meeting minutes
evidence.example: As secretary of a student society, you decide whether to use an AI tool to draft meeting minutes. You check the students' union's data policy, weigh time saved against members' privacy and accuracy, and explain your decision to the committee (for example, choosing not to upload recordings that include welfare discussions). This shows you can decide with reasons when and when not to use AI.
evidence.artefact: The decision note shared with the committee, citing the policy you checked, and the minutes approving it.
grounding: professional: Decides whether and how to use AI tools in work, within the organisation's policy, and can justify the decision. (Jisc digital capabilities: digital learning and development)

genericOutcomes.title: Policy based reasoning for using one digital tool over another
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can weigh the goals and risks of a task against a stated policy to decide which digital tool, if any, is appropriate.
genericOutcomes.example: Faced with a choice between two digital tools that a field commonly relies on, you set out, using a structured model of planning before acting, the goals the task needs to meet and the risks each tool brings. You weigh the options against a stated policy on acceptable use, and record which tool you chose and why you chose it. This demonstrates reasoned, policy-aware use of the digital tools a field relies on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written comparison of the two tools, the policy applied and the reasoned choice you made.

genericOutcomes.title: Documented decision to use or decline a digital tool
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can decide, with reference to policy and a reasoned weighing of benefits against risks, whether to use or decline a digital tool for a task.
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked whether a digital tool commonly used in your field should be used for a specific task. You check the relevant policy on its use, weigh the benefits against the risks it carries for this particular task, and record a clear decision with your reasoning, whether that decision is to use the tool or to decline it. This demonstrates using the digital tools a field relies on, with justified, policy-aware judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written decision record stating the policy checked, the reasoning weighed and the final choice made.
grounding: professional: Decides whether and how to use a digital tool in work, within policy, and can justify the decision.

capabilities.statement: Avoid the GenAI misconduct risks, and never cite GenAI as a source

evidence.title: Integrity case analysis of GenAI misconduct scenarios
evidence.example: You analyse four short scenarios of GenAI use against the six fundamental values of academic integrity set out by the International Center for Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021): honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. For each, you judge whether it risks misconduct and why citing GenAI output as a source is never acceptable (for example, a history student citing a chatbot's summary of a treaty instead of the treaty itself).
evidence.artefact: A written case analysis of four scenarios with your judgement on each and the integrity values it engages.
grounding: model: Fundamental values of academic integrity (ICAI 2021)

evidence.title: Confidentiality and attribution decision on a legal placement
evidence.example: On a placement in a law firm, you are tempted to paste a client letter into a public AI tool to summarise it. You check the firm's policy, decline because of confidentiality, and when a colleague's AI summary names a case, you find and cite the judgment itself (for example, tracing a cited precedent to the law report). This shows you avoid GenAI risks and never treat its output as a source.
evidence.artefact: A decision record signed by your supervisor, showing the policy checked and the primary sources you traced and cited.
grounding: professional: Uses AI within professional and legal rules on authorship, confidentiality and attribution.

genericOutcomes.title: Written account of why AI output cannot be a source
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify why presenting generative AI output as a citable source constitutes misconduct rather than a legitimate shortcut.
genericOutcomes.example: You set out, in a short written account, why treating a generative AI tool's output as a citable source is a form of misconduct rather than a shortcut. You explain the difference between using AI to support your thinking and presenting its output as if it were evidence, and you identify two further risks the same misuse could create. This demonstrates avoiding GenAI misconduct risks and never citing GenAI as a source.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account distinguishing AI support from AI as a false source, with two further risks identified.
grounding: model: Fundamental values of academic integrity (ICAI 2021)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Tracing a primary source instead of citing an AI summary
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can trace a claim generated by an AI tool back to its original source and cite that source instead of the AI output.
genericOutcomes.example: You come across a claim that has clearly been generated by an AI tool and that someone intends to rely on as if it were a source. Rather than repeating or citing it, you trace the original material the claim refers to, check it directly, and cite that original material instead. This demonstrates avoiding GenAI misconduct risks and never treating generative AI output as a citable source.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note tracing the claim to its original source, with the citation you used in place of the AI output.
grounding: professional: Uses AI within professional and legal rules on authorship, confidentiality and attribution.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Distinguish permitted support from unfair advantage

evidence.title: Position paper on assistive tools and fair assessment
evidence.example: You write a short position paper distinguishing support that removes a barrier from support that does the assessed work for you. Using Universal Design for Learning (CAST 2018), you argue that tools such as speech-to-text can widen access without changing what is assessed, while a paraphrasing tool may replace the skill being tested (for example, in a law coursework essay). You test your distinction against two borderline cases.
evidence.artefact: A 1,200-word position paper with two borderline cases analysed and your reasoned judgement on each.

evidence.title: Peer guidance sheet on permitted tools for an exam
evidence.example: As a peer-assisted learning leader in engineering, you are asked by students which tools are allowed in a coming open-book exam. You compare the exam regulations with the tools they mention, judge which give fair support and which an unfair advantage, and draft a guidance sheet for the module lead to check (for example, a permitted calculator versus an AI solver app).
evidence.artefact: The guidance sheet with the module lead's corrections and approval, and a note of the regulations you used.
grounding: professional: Judges whether a tool or aid is fair and permitted in a regulated assessment or practice.

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoned judgement on a borderline assistive tool
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique the evidence for and against a borderline assistive tool to reach a defensible judgement on whether its use is fair.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a tool that sits on the boundary between fair support and unfair advantage, you weigh the evidence for each side, including what the task is meant to test and what the tool actually does, before reaching a judgement. You set out your reasoning so someone else could follow and challenge it, rather than simply asserting a conclusion without support. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a reasoned judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written judgement on the borderline tool, with the evidence weighed and the reasoning set out.

genericOutcomes.title: Recommendation on a disputed tool's fairness
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can weigh what a task is meant to assess against what a disputed tool actually does, and justify a recommendation on its fairness.
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to recommend whether a specific tool should be allowed in a regulated task, and the evidence on it is mixed. You weigh what the task is meant to assess against what the tool can actually do for the person using it, state which consideration carries most weight, and make a justified recommendation. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a judgement someone else can act on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short recommendation stating the evidence weighed, the judgement reached and the reasoning behind it.
grounding: professional: Judges whether a tool or aid is fair and permitted in a regulated assessment or practice.

capabilities.statement: Weigh AI's costs and benefits as a responsible professional user

evidence.title: Triple bottom line appraisal of AI in your own practice
evidence.example: You appraise your own use of AI over one term using Elkington's (1997) triple bottom line of people, planet and profit. You weigh time saved and quality gained against energy use, data and privacy risks, and the effect on the graduate you want to become (for example, a master's architecture student deciding whether image generators belong in early concept work). You end with a justified personal policy.
evidence.artefact: A reflective appraisal with a costs and benefits table under the three headings and your written personal AI policy.

evidence.title: Options appraisal of an AI chatbot for a small firm
evidence.example: On a consultancy project for a small business, you are asked whether it should adopt an AI chatbot for customer enquiries. You weigh costs, data protection, environmental impact and effects on staff against expected benefits, disclose any AI you used in the analysis, and make a justified recommendation (for example, advising a family-run travel agent to trial the tool only for booking changes).
evidence.artefact: The options appraisal report with your recommendation, AI-use disclosure and the client's written response.
grounding: professional: Assesses the costs, risks and sustainability of adopting a technology against its benefits.

genericOutcomes.title: Ethical weighing of a technology's costs against its benefits
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can synthesise a technology's ethical costs, such as environmental impact or effect on roles, with its practical benefits to reach a justified position.
genericOutcomes.example: You are given a technology that raises a genuine ethical question, such as its environmental cost or its effect on people's work, and asked to weigh this against its practical benefits. Using an established framework for balancing social, environmental and economic considerations, you set out the competing factors and reach a reasoned position on whether the benefits justify the costs. This demonstrates recognising and acting on the ethical issues a technology raises.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written appraisal weighing the technology's ethical costs against its benefits, with a reasoned conclusion.

genericOutcomes.title: Ethically justified recommendation on adopting a technology
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can assess the ethical costs and practical benefits of adopting a technology and justify a recommendation that withstands disagreement.
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to recommend whether a technology should be adopted, and the ethical costs, including its environmental impact and effect on people's roles, are not trivial. You weigh these costs against the practical benefits, state clearly where you draw the line, and put forward a recommendation you can justify to someone who disagrees with it. This demonstrates recognising and acting on the ethical responsibilities a technology decision carries.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short recommendation record stating the ethical costs weighed, the benefits considered and your justified decision.
grounding: professional: Assesses the costs, risks and sustainability of adopting a technology against its benefits.
